analysis.one_liner: Ends courts' practice of deferring to federal agencies' interpretations of the laws they enforce.
analysis.headline: The House Judiciary Committee never acted on the bill, and it died at the end of the 115th Congress without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, when a court reviews a federal agency's decision, it usually accepts the agency's own reading of the statute it administers. This bill would change that: courts would have to decide from scratch, with no weight given to the agency's interpretation, every legal question involving agency rules and the statutes behind them. That would make it much easier for regulated businesses to get agency rules thrown out in court. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated industries — manufacturers, energy companies, financial firms, and others subject to federal rules — would gain a powerful new tool: any business challenging an agency rule would no longer face a court that presumes the agency's legal reading is reasonable. Agency rules on the environment, workplace safety, consumer protection, and health care would face easier court challenges, and new rules would be harder to defend.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Administrative Procedure Act so that a reviewing court must decide de novo — from the beginning, with no deference to the agency — all questions of law, including the meaning of constitutional provisions, statutes, and agency rules [S2] [S3].
It applies to any civil action for judicial review of agency action, and no other law could exempt a case from this standard except by naming this section specifically [S3].
Sponsors framed the change as a separation-of-powers measure, arguing that courts, not executive-branch agencies, should decide what the law means [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Federal agencies would lose much of their ability to interpret ambiguous statutes, and the public rules built on that ability — pollution limits, safety standards, benefit rules — would become more vulnerable to litigation and invalidation. People who rely on those protections would bear the cost if the bill passed, and regulated industries would bear it in reverse today only as a lost opportunity.

drawbacks.text: Courts would face renewed litigation over nearly every significant agency rule, since the bill strips deference across the board and bars exemptions, which would inject legal uncertainty into areas like environmental and financial regulation [S3].

Proponents' good-faith objection to the status quo is real: deferring to agencies lets unelected officials effectively decide what the law means, and the bill's backers argued the Constitution assigns that job to courts [S1]. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that judges lack the technical expertise agencies use when filling in the details of broad statutes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have shifted power from executive agencies to federal courts. That carries a genuine constitutional argument, but its practical effect would be to make agency rules — the product of statutes that require expert implementation — easier for regulated parties to defeat in court, with the losses falling on the people those rules protect. The shift would be broad, immediate, and hard to unwind.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, sent to a subcommittee two days later, and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Ratcliffe introduced the bill on January 3, 2017, the first day of the 115th Congress, with 50 original Republican cosponsors [S1] [S3].
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on January 3, 2017, and on January 5 it went to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law [S5].
No further action was taken: the bill never reached the full committee or the House floor, and it expired when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The existing system of agency deference stayed intact, so the businesses that would have used the new standard to challenge federal rules gained nothing, and the regulatory protections ordinary people rely on were left standing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Rules and the people they protect

for.name: Rep. John Ratcliffe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 115th Congress and recruited original cosponsors.

for.name: 65 of 241 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Republican, and 50 signed on as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: Rep. Bob Goodlatte
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor the day the bill was introduced.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on January 5, 2017, and never scheduled a hearing or a markup, keeping it off the House floor for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 65 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past a subcommittee referral [S4].

industries.note: The bill would hand these businesses a far easier path to overturning federal rules, since courts would no longer defer to agencies' legal interpretations. Their gain would come at the cost of the pollution, safety, and consumer protections those rules provide.

industries.industry: Federal regulatory agencies (environmental, workplace, consumer, health)
industries.note: Agencies would lose the deference courts currently give their statutory interpretations, weakening their ability to implement the laws Congress wrote. That loss would fall most directly on the public those agencies regulate on behalf of.
